items.title: Laplacian kernel on Morgan count vectors for SVR
items.spec: In fit_predict, replace the min/max Tanimoto kernel used by the precomputed SVR with a Laplacian kernel K(a,b) = exp(-gamma * L1(a,b)) on the same 2048-bit radius-2 count vectors, where gamma = 1 / (mean pairwise L1 distance over the training set). Build the training and test kernel matrices with scipy.spatial.distance.cdist(metric='cityblock'). Keep C=5.0, epsilon=0.1, and the rank-normalized standardized target unchanged. The XGBoost branch and the rank-sum blend stay as they are.

items.title: Blend by mean of z-scored predictions instead of rank sum
items.spec: Keep both members (XGBoost on descriptors plus fingerprints, and the Tanimoto SVR) exactly as in train.py. Change only the final combination: standardize each member's test predictions to zero mean and unit variance using the statistics of that member's own test predictions, average the two z-scores with equal weight, and return the result. Do not rank the final average. This tests whether preserving the magnitude of each model's output beats rank averaging.

items.title: Nearest-neighbour target-encoding feature for XGBoost
items.spec: Before fitting XGBoost, add one feature per molecule: the mean rank-normalized target of its k=10 most similar training molecules by min/max Tanimoto on the radius-2 count fingerprint. For training rows, compute this with an inner 5-fold split so a molecule never uses its own label. For test rows, use all training molecules. Append this column to the existing xgb_features matrix. Everything else (XGBoost settings, SVR, blend) stays the same.

items.title: XGBoost with pairwise ranking objective
items.spec: Replace the XGBRegressor in the XGBoost branch with xgboost.XGBRanker using objective='rank:pairwise', all training molecules in a single query group, and the same tree settings (max_depth 4, 600 trees, lr 0.03, subsample 0.7, colsample 0.3, min_child_weight 3, reg_lambda 5). Feed it the rank-normalized target as relevance labels cast to integers in 0..20 (multiply by 20 and round). Predictions are used only for rank-blending, so the scale does not matter. The SVR branch and blend stay the same.

items.title: MACCS-keys Tanimoto kernel for a second SVR
items.spec: Compute MACCS keys (rdkit.Chem.MACCSkeys.GenMACCSKeys) for all molecules as 167-bit vectors. Build a min/max count-style Tanimoto kernel on these bits, reusing the existing tanimoto() helper. Train a second precomputed SVR (C=5.0, epsilon=0.1) on the same rank-standardized target and add its rank-normalized test prediction to the blend with equal weight alongside the existing RF/XGB and Morgan SVR members. Do not change the Morgan kernel.

items.title: Radius-1 Morgan count kernel for SVR
items.spec: Use Morgan count fingerprints at radius 1 with 1024 bits (rdFingerprintGenerator.GetMorganGenerator(radius=1, fpSize=1024)) as the input to the existing min/max Tanimoto kernel for the precomputed SVR, in place of the radius-2 2048-bit features. Keep C=5.0, epsilon=0.1 and the rank-standardized target. The XGBoost branch and blend remain unchanged. This tests whether a coarser, more generalizing substructure representation helps on unseen scaffolds.

items.title: Residual XGBoost on out-of-fold SVR predictions
items.spec: Inside fit_predict, compute out-of-fold SVR predictions on the training set with an inner 5-fold KFold (shuffle, random_state=seed) using the existing precomputed Tanimoto SVR. Fit the XGBoost model on descriptor plus fingerprint features to the residual target (rank target minus the out-of-fold SVR prediction), instead of the rank target. For test molecules, add the SVR prediction fitted on all training data to the XGBoost residual prediction. Blend the resulting prediction with the plain SVR prediction by rank average, equal weights.

items.title: Random-subspace SVR ensemble over fingerprint bit subsets
items.spec: Build 10 precomputed SVRs. Each one uses a random 50 percent of the 2048 Morgan count bits, selected with np.random.default_rng(seed + k) for k in 0..9, and its own min/max Tanimoto kernel computed on that column subset. Each SVR uses C=5.0, epsilon=0.1 and the rank-standardized target. Average the 10 test predictions (rank-normalized) and use the result in place of the single SVR in the blend, keeping the XGBoost branch and the equal-weight rank blend unchanged.

items.title: Log-target SVR as a diverse blend member
items.spec: Add a third member to the blend: a precomputed Tanimoto SVR (C=5.0, epsilon=0.1) fitted not on the rank target but on the standardized log of the raw training values, computed as log(max(train_y, small_positive)) if all train_y are positive, otherwise on the raw values after a sign-preserving log1p transform. Rank-normalize its test predictions and add them to the existing rank-sum blend with equal weight. The Morgan SVR on the rank target and the XGBoost branch remain as they are.

items.title: Scaffold-free bagging of XGBoost over bootstrap molecules
items.spec: Train 5 XGBoost models in fit_predict, each on a bootstrap sample of the training molecules drawn with np.random.default_rng(seed + k), using the same rank target and descriptor plus fingerprint features and the existing tree settings. Average their test predictions before rank-blending. Keep the SVR branch and the equal-weight rank blend unchanged. This is a bootstrap-bagging variant of the seed-bagging already tried, using row resampling instead of seed-only variation.

items.title: Blend weights 0.6 SVR / 0.4 XGB
items.spec: In fit_predict, change the final return to 0.4*rankdata(p_rf)/len(p_rf) + 0.6*rankdata(p_svr)/len(p_svr) so the Tanimoto SVR gets more weight. No other changes.

items.title: Tune SVR C to 10 and epsilon 0.05
items.spec: Change the SVR to C=10.0, epsilon=0.05 on the rank-standardized target. Leave everything else unchanged.

items.title: Lower SVR C to 2 with epsilon 0.1
items.spec: Change the SVR C from 5.0 to 2.0 for stronger regularization on the min/max Tanimoto kernel. Keep other settings the same.

items.title: Power-transformed Tanimoto kernel
items.spec: In tanimoto(), return the kernel raised to the power 2 (num**2) before it is passed to the SVR. It stays positive semidefinite, and it sharpens similarity toward near neighbours. Apply it to both train-train and test-train kernels.

items.title: Seed-bagged SVR on subsamples
items.spec: Fit 5 SVRs, each on a random 80% subsample of the training rows. Draw the subsamples with np.random.default_rng(seed). Slice the precomputed train kernel for each one, and average the test predictions before ranking. Compute the kernels once.

items.title: Add XGB on pairwise-rank objective
items.spec: Add a second XGBRegressor-like member using XGBRanker is not suitable, so instead use XGBRegressor with objective 'reg:pseudohubererror' on the same features and the rank target. Rank-average it with the existing XGB prediction inside the XGB branch before blending with the SVR.

items.title: Scaffold-aware sample weights
items.spec: Compute the Murcko scaffold for each training molecule. Give each molecule a sample_weight of 1/sqrt(scaffold count) and normalize the weights to mean 1. Pass the weights to XGB.fit and to SVR.fit as sample_weight.

items.title: Atom-pair count kernel averaged into SVR kernel
items.spec: Compute atom-pair count fingerprints (rdFingerprintGenerator.GetAtomPairGenerator, fpSize 2048). Compute their min/max kernel. Average it with the Morgan kernel at 50/50 and fit a single SVR on the averaged kernel. Keep the XGB branch unchanged.

items.title: Stronger XGB column and row regularization
items.spec: Change XGBRegressor to colsample_bytree=0.15, colsample_bynode=0.7, subsample=0.6, and reg_alpha=1. Keep depth 4, 600 trees and lr 0.03.

items.title: Log1p of counts in Tanimoto kernel features
items.spec: In featurize(), apply np.log1p to the Morgan count array before it is returned. The min/max kernel then downweights high-count bits. Leave the XGB features unchanged.

items.title: Replicate the incumbent unchanged
items.spec: Make no change to train.py and run the job as-is to get a second measurement of the current incumbent (reported 0.4718 from a single run, noise sd ~0.0070). Several recent candidates came in within 0.004-0.006 of the incumbent and were rejected on one run each, so the incumbent's own value is the least certain number in the table and is the reference every future delta is measured against. The edit should be a no-op touch (for example a comment line added at the top of the file, or no edit at all if the harness permits), and the job must otherwise produce bit-identical modeling behaviour. Deliverable is just the loss, to be averaged with the existing 0.4718.

items.title: Weight the blend 0.6 SVR / 0.4 XGB
items.spec: The final line of fit_predict currently adds the two rank-normalized predictions with equal weight. Change it to a weighted sum: 0.6 * rankdata(p_svr)/len(p_svr) + 0.4 * rankdata(p_rf)/len(p_rf). Nothing else changes. Rationale: the Tanimoto-kernel SVR is the member that works on unseen scaffolds by direct similarity, while the tree model has repeatedly resisted improvement (many XGB/CatBoost/RF swaps all landed at or above the incumbent), which suggests the tree branch may be the weaker of the two and is being over-weighted. Keep the change to a single arithmetic line so the diff stays trivial.

items.title: Pick the SVR C by a small inner CV
items.spec: Inside fit_predict, before fitting the final SVR, choose the regularization constant C by an inner 5-fold cross-validation on the training set only. Compute the train-train min/max Tanimoto kernel once, then for each C in [1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0] run a 5-fold KFold(shuffle=True, random_state=seed) over the kernel rows and columns (slicing the precomputed kernel, never recomputing it), scoring each fold by Spearman correlation of the held-out predictions against the standardized rank target. Pick the C with the best mean Spearman, refit the SVR on the full training kernel with that C, and use it in the blend exactly as now. Keep epsilon at 0.1. This is cheap because the kernel is reused, and C has never been tuned since it was set to 5.0 by hand.

items.title: Bag the SVR over bootstrap resamples
items.spec: Replace the single Tanimoto-kernel SVR with an average of 8 SVRs fitted on bootstrap resamples of the training set. Compute the full train-train and test-train min/max Tanimoto kernels once. For each of 8 bags, draw a bootstrap sample of row indices with a seed-derived RandomState, slice the kernel to those rows and columns, fit SVR(kernel='precomputed', C=5.0, epsilon=0.1) on the standardized rank target of those rows, predict the test set from the corresponding test-train kernel columns, and rank-normalize each bag's prediction. Average the 8 rank vectors to get p_svr, then blend with the XGB branch as before. Bagging should reduce the variance of the kernel model without touching its bias, and the cost is small because the expensive kernel computation is shared.

items.title: Use nu-SVR instead of epsilon-SVR
items.spec: Swap the epsilon-SVR for sklearn.svm.NuSVR with kernel='precomputed', nu=0.5, C=5.0, on exactly the same min/max Tanimoto kernel and the same standardized rank target, keeping the blend unchanged. With a rank target the residual scale is fixed and known, so the fraction-of-support-vectors parameterization of nu-SVR is a more natural fit than a hand-set epsilon tube of 0.1 in rank-sd units; nu directly controls how much of the training set contributes. If NuSVR is noticeably slower, cap it with max_iter left at default and nothing else; the kernel is only 970x970 so runtime is not a concern.

items.title: Rank-average three separate kernel SVRs
items.spec: Earlier attempts averaged several Tanimoto kernels into one matrix before fitting a single SVR (FCFP4 and atom-pair variants, both near noise). Do the opposite: fit three independent SVRs, one per kernel, and combine them at the rank level. Build three count-feature matrices for train and test: ECFP4 counts (radius 2, 2048 bits, as now), FCFP4 counts (radius 2, 2048 bits, with the feature-invariant atom generator), and atom-pair counts (2048 bits). For each, compute the min/max Tanimoto kernel and fit SVR(kernel='precomputed', C=5.0, epsilon=0.1) on the standardized rank target, then rank-normalize its test predictions. The combined SVR prediction is the mean of the three rank vectors; blend it 50/50 with the XGB rank prediction as now. Averaging at the decision level preserves each kernel's own geometry instead of blurring them into one metric.

items.title: Add a seed-bagged dart LightGBM as a third member
items.spec: Add a third blend member: a LightGBM regressor with boosting_type='dart', averaged over 3 seeds. Reuse the existing xgb_features matrices (compute them once and pass them to both the XGBoost and the LightGBM, so the expensive featurization is not repeated). Use roughly n_estimators=600, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=15, feature_fraction=0.3, bagging_fraction=0.7, bagging_freq=1, min_child_samples=10, drop_rate=0.1, n_jobs=8, verbose=-1, with random_state=seed+i for i in 0..2, fitted on the same rank target. Rank-normalize the mean of the three predictions and return the equally weighted sum of the three rank vectors (XGB, SVR, dart LGBM). Dart's dropout makes its errors less correlated with plain gradient boosting than the CatBoost/RF/LightGBM-gbdt third members already tried.

items.title: Scaffold-frequency sample weights for the tree model
items.spec: Because every fold tests on unseen Murcko scaffolds, training molecules from large scaffold families are effectively redundant and dominate the tree model's fit. Compute the Bemis-Murcko scaffold SMILES of each training molecule with rdkit.Chem.Scaffolds.MurckoScaffold.MurckoScaffoldSmiles, count how many training molecules share each scaffold, and pass sample_weight = 1/count (or 1/sqrt(count) if that is simpler to justify; pick 1/count) to the XGBoost fit, normalized so the weights average 1. Leave the SVR branch, the features, the target transform and the blend untouched. This makes the tree model's effective training distribution closer to the scaffold-balanced test distribution.

items.title: Smooth the rank target with Tanimoto neighbours
items.spec: The measured clearance values are noisy, and the loss only cares about ordering, so lightly smoothing the target along the chemical-similarity graph may help both members. After computing the uniform rank target y, build the train-train min/max Tanimoto kernel on the Morgan count features (it is already needed for the SVR, so reuse it). For each training molecule find its 5 nearest neighbours by that kernel, excluding itself, and replace y_i with 0.8*y_i + 0.2*mean(y of those 5 neighbours). Re-rank-normalize the smoothed vector to keep it on [0,1] and use it as the fit target for both the XGBoost and the SVR. Everything else, including prediction and blending, stays the same.

items.title: Power-transform the Tanimoto kernel
items.spec: Sharpen the SVR's similarity measure by exponentiating the min/max Tanimoto kernel elementwise: after computing K = tanimoto(A, B), use K**3 (and the same transform for both the train-train and test-train matrices) as the precomputed kernel. A raw min/max kernel over count fingerprints is fairly flat -- most pairs sit in a narrow mid-similarity band -- so cubing it increases the contrast between genuine near-neighbours and the bulk, which is what matters when a fold tests on unseen scaffolds. Elementwise powers of a Tanimoto kernel remain positive semidefinite, so no regularization hack is needed. Keep C=5.0 and epsilon=0.1 and the rest of the pipeline identical; implement it as a one-line change inside or just after tanimoto().

items.title: Replicate the incumbent unchanged
items.spec: Make no change to train.py at all; submit the current file as-is so the harness runs it a second time. The incumbent score of 0.4718 comes from a single run, and the per-job noise sd is about 0.0070, so the true loss could plausibly be anywhere in roughly 0.458-0.486. Several recent candidates (CatBoost third member 0.4678, FCFP4 kernel 0.4637/0.4771, ECFP6 kernel 0.4658, averaged Avalon kernel 0.4683) scored below the incumbent but were rejected as within noise; whether they are real improvements depends on where the incumbent actually sits. A second independent run of the incumbent halves the uncertainty on the reference point and makes every future accept/reject decision sharper. No code edit is needed, only a re-run.

items.title: Tune the SVR regularization: C=2 and epsilon=0.05
items.spec: In fit_predict, change the precomputed SVR from SVR(kernel='precomputed', C=5.0, epsilon=0.1) to SVR(kernel='precomputed', C=2.0, epsilon=0.05). The SVR half of the blend has never had its hyperparameters touched since it was introduced in slot 0, yet it carries half the blend weight. The target is a rank transform scaled to roughly [0,1] and then standardized to unit variance before fitting, so epsilon=0.1 is a wide insensitive tube relative to the spread of y, and C=5 is fairly weak regularization for a 776-row kernel matrix (the per-fold training size). Lowering C increases regularization and lowering epsilon lets the model fit more of the rank ordering rather than ignoring differences inside the tube. Keep everything else identical: same kernel, same features, same XGBoost branch, same equal-weight rank blend.

items.title: Shift the blend weight toward the SVR (0.6/0.4)
items.spec: The final line of fit_predict currently returns rankdata(p_rf)/len(p_rf) + rankdata(p_svr)/len(p_svr), an exactly equal blend. Change it to a weighted blend favoring the SVR: 0.6*rankdata(p_svr)/len(p_svr) + 0.4*rankdata(p_rf)/len(p_rf). The two members have never had their relative weight varied, and there is reason to think the SVR deserves more: the Tanimoto min/max kernel generalizes across unseen Murcko scaffolds by direct structural similarity, which is exactly what the scaffold-grouped folds test, whereas the tree model keys on descriptor thresholds learned from the scaffolds present in training. Since Spearman only cares about ordering, the weighting acts purely on the relative influence of the two rank vectors. Keep both members and all their hyperparameters unchanged; only the two coefficients in the return statement change.

items.title: Average three SVR fits over bootstrap resamples of the training set
items.spec: Replace the single precomputed SVR fit with an average over three bootstrap replicates. Compute the full kernels Ktr = tanimoto(Xtr, Xtr) and Kte = tanimoto(Xte, Xtr) once, as now. Then for b in range(3), draw a bootstrap sample of row indices idx with a numpy Generator seeded by seed+b, fit SVR(kernel='precomputed', C=5.0, epsilon=0.1) on Ktr[np.ix_(idx, idx)] with the correspondingly indexed standardized target, predict on Kte[:, idx], rank-normalize that prediction, and accumulate. Use the mean of the three rank vectors as p_svr in the final blend. Bagging a kernel method reduces the variance that comes from individual support vectors in a small 970-molecule dataset, and the kernel slices are cheap because the expensive min/max computation is done only once. Three replicates keep the runtime well inside the 10-minute budget.

items.title: Fit the blend weight by inner cross-validation instead of fixing it
items.spec: Choose the blend weight from the training data rather than hard-coding 0.5/0.5. Inside fit_predict, after building features, run a 5-fold KFold (shuffle=True, random_state=seed) over the training molecules; in each inner fold fit both the XGBoost and the precomputed SVR on the inner-train part and predict the inner-test part, collecting out-of-fold predictions for both members over all training molecules. Rank-normalize each out-of-fold vector, then scan weights w in np.arange(0, 1.01, 0.1), compute the Spearman correlation of w*svr_oof + (1-w)*xgb_oof against the rank target, and keep the best w. Finally fit both members on the full training set as now and return w*rankdata(p_svr)/n + (1-w)*rankdata(p_rf)/n. This lets the data decide the weight per fold instead of assuming equal contribution. Reduce the XGBoost to 300 trees inside the inner loop only, to keep the 15 fits inside the time limit.

items.title: Sharpen the Tanimoto kernel with an exponential transform
items.spec: Keep the min/max Tanimoto similarity computation in tanimoto() but pass the result through an exponential before the SVR sees it: in fit_predict, wrap both kernel matrices as np.exp(-GAMMA*(1.0 - K)) with GAMMA = 3.0, where K is the raw min/max similarity. Add GAMMA as a module-level setting. The raw Tanimoto kernel is close to linear in similarity, so a molecule at similarity 0.3 still exerts meaningful pull on the prediction; the exponential form compresses the influence of distant molecules and emphasizes close structural neighbors, which is the regime where measured hepatocyte clearance actually transfers. This is the standard way to turn a similarity into a Laplacian-style kernel and keeps the matrix positive semi-definite in practice. A related exp(-2*(1-T)) kernel was tried in slot 33, but only as an extra third blend member on Avalon features, never as a replacement for the existing Morgan-count kernel of the current SVR.

items.title: Average predictions over bagged XGBoost feature subsets
items.spec: Replace the single XGBoost fit with an average over three fits that each see a random two-thirds of the feature columns. Compute Xtr_f = xgb_features(train_smiles) and Xte_f = xgb_features(test_smiles) once at the top of fit_predict (the current code calls xgb_features three times, which is wasteful and should be fixed anyway). Then for b in range(3), use a numpy Generator seeded by seed+b to choose a random subset of two-thirds of the column indices, fit the existing XGBRegressor configuration with random_state=seed+b on Xtr_f[:, cols], predict Xte_f[:, cols], rank-normalize, and average the three rank vectors into p_rf. The feature matrix mixes descriptors, Morgan counts, Avalon counts and ErG into several thousand columns of very different character, and column bagging decorrelates the members more than reseeding alone does (a plain 5-seed average scored 0.4722, i.e. no gain). Caching the features offsets most of the added cost.

items.title: Weight training molecules by inverse scaffold frequency
items.spec: Add scaffold-frequency sample weights to the XGBoost fit. Import MurckoScaffold from rdkit.Chem.Scaffolds, compute the Murcko scaffold SMILES for every training molecule, count how many training molecules share each scaffold, and build weights w_i = 1/sqrt(count of molecule i's scaffold), normalized to mean 1. Pass these as sample_weight to model.fit. Because the harness keeps a whole scaffold inside one fold, each test fold is made of skeletons the model has never seen, so what matters is learning structure-transferable signal rather than fitting the few over-represented scaffold families well. Down-weighting large scaffold clusters stops a handful of congeneric series from dominating the loss surface and should push the trees toward splits that generalize across skeletons. Leave the SVR branch, the rank target and the blend untouched so the effect is attributable to the weights alone.

items.title: Add a second SVR on a 3D-free shape and polarity kernel
items.spec: Add a third rank-blended member: a precomputed SVR on a min/max kernel built from a compact, strictly physicochemical feature block rather than substructure counts. For each molecule compute a vector of about 20 interpretable quantities that drive hepatic metabolism: MolLogP, MolMR, TPSA, NumHDonors, NumHAcceptors, NumRotatableBonds, FractionCSP3, HeavyAtomCount, NumAromaticRings, NumAliphaticRings, NumSaturatedRings, RingCount, NHOHCount, NOCount, BertzCT, BalabanJ, HallKierAlpha, Kappa1, Kappa2, Kappa3. Rank-normalize each column across the combined train+test set so all features land in [0,1] and are non-negative, which makes the existing tanimoto() min/max routine a valid kernel on them. Fit SVR(kernel='precomputed', C=5.0, epsilon=0.1) on the standardized rank target and blend its rank-normalized prediction as an equal third of the final sum. Earlier descriptor-based extra members used Ridge, MLP or an RBF SVR; a min/max kernel on rank-scaled physchem columns is a different and better-matched geometry for these features.

items.title: Average each molecule's prediction over its own randomized SMILES
items.spec: Add test-time augmentation at the featurization level. Write a helper that, given a SMILES string and a seed, returns a list of K=5 equivalent SMILES by calling Chem.MolToSmiles(mol, doRandom=True, canonical=False) with the RDKit random seed set deterministically from the harness seed, always including the canonical form as one of the K. In fit_predict, build the XGBoost test matrix by featurizing all K variants of every test molecule, predicting each, and averaging the K predictions per molecule before rank-normalizing. Train on canonical SMILES only. Most descriptors and all fingerprints are graph-canonical and so invariant to SMILES writing order, which means the averaging is a no-op for them; the point is to catch and smooth any order-dependent descriptor columns in Descriptors.descList and to verify empirically that the feature pipeline is genuinely invariant. If the loss is unchanged within noise, that is itself a useful negative result that rules out a whole class of worry. Keep the SVR branch and the blend unchanged.
